1: The risen Jesus teaches the apostles for forty days, promises the Holy Spirit and is taken up to heaven. The apostles return to Jerusalem and pray with Mary. They choose Matthias to replace Judas.
The Church begins by waiting in prayer. The apostles fill Judas's place because their office is meant to continue.
2: The Holy Spirit comes with a sound like wind and tongues of fire. The apostles speak and people of every language understand. Peter preaches that God raised Jesus, and three thousand are baptised. The believers share everything and devote themselves to the apostles' teaching and the breaking of bread.
This is often called the birthday of the Church. The four marks of its life in verse 42 are still what parish life is made of.
3: At the Temple gate Peter tells a man lame from birth, "Silver and gold I have none, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk." Peter then explains to the crowd that the power is Jesus'.
The apostles continue Jesus' own works in his name. The miracle is a doorway to preaching.
4: Peter and John are hauled before the council and ordered to stop speaking about Jesus. Peter replies that there is no other name by which we are saved, and that they cannot keep quiet about what they have seen. The community prays for boldness and shares its goods.
Ordinary fishermen stand up to the highest court. Their courage comes from the Spirit, not from education.
5: Ananias and Sapphira; the apostles flogged

A couple lies about a gift to the Church and both fall dead. The apostles work many signs, are jailed, and freed by an angel. Gamaliel advises the council to wait and see. The apostles are beaten and leave rejoicing.
"We must obey God rather than men." Lying to the Church is treated as lying to the Holy Spirit.
6: Greek-speaking widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution. The apostles appoint seven men, including Stephen, by laying hands on them. Stephen's preaching stirs up enemies who accuse him falsely.
The Church has traditionally seen here the beginning of the order of deacons: service of the poor so that the apostles can pray and preach.
7: Stephen retells Israel's history to show that the people have always resisted God's messengers. The council drags him out and stones him. He dies seeing heaven opened and praying, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." A young man named Saul looks on.
Stephen dies as Jesus died, forgiving his killers. His prayer will bear fruit in Saul.
8: Persecution scatters the believers, who preach wherever they go. Philip evangelises Samaria, and Peter and John lay hands on the baptised so that they receive the Spirit. Philip explains Isaiah to an Ethiopian official and baptises him.
Persecution spreads the faith instead of stopping it. The Ethiopian's question, "How can I understand unless someone guides me?", shows why Scripture needs the Church.
9: On the road to Damascus a light throws Saul to the ground and a voice says, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" Blinded, he is led into the city, where Ananias baptises him. He begins preaching Christ. Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha.
Jesus says "me", not "my followers": he and his Church are one. The fiercest enemy becomes the greatest missionary.
10: A Roman centurion named Cornelius is told in a vision to send for Peter. Peter has a vision of animals and hears, "What God has made clean, do not call unclean." He preaches in Cornelius's house, the Spirit falls on the Gentiles, and they are baptised.
"God shows no partiality." The Church is for every nation, and it is Peter who opens that door.
11: Peter defends baptising Gentiles before the believers in Jerusalem. A great mixed church grows at Antioch, where Barnabas and Saul teach for a year. The disciples are first called Christians there.
The name "Christian" is given in a church of Jews and Gentiles together.
12: King Herod kills James the brother of John and jails Peter. The Church prays without stopping, and an angel leads Peter out past the guards. Herod later dies after accepting praise as a god.
The first apostle is martyred, and another is rescued. Both are in God's hands.
13: The Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul, now called Paul. They preach in Cyprus and in Antioch of Pisidia, where Paul tells the synagogue that Jesus is the promised Saviour. When many Jews reject the message, they turn to the Gentiles.
Mission begins from prayer and fasting. The pattern of Paul's work is set: to the Jew first, then to the Gentile.
14: At Lystra Paul heals a lame man, and the crowd tries to offer sacrifice to him and Barnabas as gods. Soon after, Paul is stoned and left for dead. He gets up, goes on, and returns to strengthen the new churches and appoint elders.
"Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." Paul appoints leaders so the churches will last.
15: Some insist that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. The apostles and elders meet. Peter speaks, James agrees, and they send a letter: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" not to impose that burden.
This is the model for every later Church council. Salvation is by the grace of Jesus, not by the old Law.
16: Paul takes Timothy with him and, after a vision, crosses to Macedonia. At Philippi Lydia believes. Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed, sing hymns at midnight, and after an earthquake the jailer and his household are baptised.
The Gospel reaches Europe. Whole households are baptised together.
17: After trouble in Thessalonica and Beroea, Paul reaches Athens. He speaks to the philosophers on the Areopagus about their altar "to an unknown God" and announces the resurrection. Some mock, some believe.
Paul starts from what his hearers already know and leads them to Christ. Faith and reason are not enemies.
18: A year and a half in Corinth

Paul works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla. The Lord tells him in a vision not to be afraid. He is cleared by the governor Gallio. Apollos, an eloquent preacher, is taught more accurately by Priscilla and Aquila.
"I have many people in this city." God encourages his worker when the task looks hopeless.
19: Paul baptises disciples who had only known John's baptism and lays hands on them. He teaches in Ephesus for two years. Converts burn their books of magic. Silversmiths who make shrines of Artemis start a riot because business is falling.
The Gospel changes what people buy and how they live, so it threatens those who profit from idols.
20: Farewell to the elders of Ephesus

At Troas Paul preaches late into the night on the first day of the week, and a young man who falls from a window is restored. At Miletus he says goodbye to the Ephesian elders and warns them to guard the flock.
Christians already gather on Sunday to break bread. "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
21: Despite warnings, Paul goes up to Jerusalem. He is seized in the Temple by a mob and rescued by Roman soldiers, who chain him.
Paul is ready to die for the name of Jesus. Like his Lord, he goes to Jerusalem knowing what waits there.
22: From the steps Paul addresses the crowd in their own language and describes his conversion. They shout him down when he mentions the Gentiles. About to be flogged, he reveals that he is a Roman citizen.
Paul's best argument is his own changed life.
23: Before the council; a plot uncovered
Paul divides the council by declaring his hope in the resurrection. The Lord tells him he must bear witness in Rome. His nephew warns of a plot to kill him, and he is taken under guard to Caesarea.
God protects Paul by ordinary means: a nephew's sharp ears and Roman soldiers.
24: Paul answers the charges before the governor Felix. Felix listens to him about justice, self-control and the coming judgement, becomes afraid, and keeps him in prison for two years hoping for a bribe.
Felix hears the truth and puts it off for "a convenient time" that never comes.
25: The new governor Festus hears the case. To avoid being sent back to Jerusalem, Paul uses his right as a citizen and appeals to the emperor. Festus consults King Agrippa.
Paul uses the legal rights he has. They become the road that takes the Gospel to Rome.
26: Paul tells Agrippa how the risen Jesus appeared to him and sent him to the Gentiles. Festus says he is mad. Agrippa says Paul could have been set free if he had not appealed.
Paul in chains is freer than the rulers judging him. He wishes they all had what he has.
27: Paul sails for Rome as a prisoner. A violent storm drives the ship for fourteen days. Paul assures everyone that an angel has promised no life will be lost. The ship breaks up on a reef, and all 276 on board reach land.
In the crisis the prisoner becomes the leader. God's promise holds in the storm.
28: On Malta Paul shakes off a viper unharmed and heals the sick. He reaches Rome and lives under guard for two years, welcoming all who come and teaching about Jesus openly.
The book ends with the Gospel being preached at the centre of the empire. The story is left open because the mission continues.
